lesson.text: Quick memory: what are volunteers? (People who help without being paid.) Children can be volunteers too. Today: ways to help your community, and how to plan a helping project.

Ways children can help: pick up litter with gloves and a grown-up, or plant flowers. Collect food for people who need it, or read to younger children. Give away books and toys you have outgrown, or help a neighbour.

A good project starts with a real need. Look and ask: Is the park messy? Do birds need food in winter? Does an older neighbour need help with shopping? Ask the people you want to help what would help most.
Plan it: What will we do? Who will help? When and where? What do we need? How will we stay safe? Which grown-up will help us?

Worked example: Mimi's group plans a litter pick. Need: rubbish in the park. Team: 4 friends and a grown-up. Kit: gloves, bags and litter pickers. Date: Saturday morning. Safety: stay together, and never touch sharp things.

Afterwards, check what changed: count the bags of rubbish, take before and after photos, or ask people what they think. Last month the group filled 6 bags; this month only 2, so the park is staying cleaner.
In many schools in Japan, children clean their own classrooms each day. The United Nations agreed 17 Global Goals in 2015. They include no hunger, clean water and caring for the planet.
Try it in the world: plan a helping project in a world you share: build a shelter for travellers, plant a garden for everyone, or fix a broken bridge. Next: a big question about the truth.

exercises.hint: Think of people who plant trees in the park for free.
choices: someone who helps without being paid
exercises.explain: A volunteer helps others without being paid.

exercises.prompt: Children are too young to help their community.
exercises.explain: False: children can pick up litter, plant flowers, read to younger children and much more.

exercises.prompt: Which of these helps the community?
exercises.hint: Which one makes the place better for others?
choices: giving outgrown books to a library
exercises.explain: Giving outgrown books lets other children read them.

exercises.prompt: What should you wear to pick up litter?
exercises.hint: Litter can be dirty or sharp.
exercises.explain: Gloves keep your hands safe; a grown-up and litter pickers help too.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a helping project in order.
exercises.hint: You can't plan before you know the need.
exercises.explain: Notice a need, ask people, plan, do it, then check what changed.

exercises.prompt: Match each need to a helping project.
exercises.explain: A messy park: a litter pick. Hungry families: a food collection. Birds in winter: a feeder. Younger children: reading to them.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: safe, or not safe on a litter pick?
exercises.hint: What keeps everyone from getting hurt?
exercises.explain: Safe: gloves, staying together and a grown-up. Not safe: broken glass, going off alone and walking in the road.

exercises.prompt: The group wants 50 books for the school library. They have 32. How many more do they need?
exercises.hint: Take what they have away from the goal.

exercises.prompt: Why ask people what would help them most?
exercises.hint: Help works best when it fits the need.
choices: so the help is what they really need
exercises.explain: Asking makes sure your project helps in the way people actually need.

exercises.prompt: How could Mimi's group show that their litter pick worked?
choices: compare bags and photos, before and after
exercises.explain: Counting the bags and comparing before and after photos shows what changed.

exercises.prompt: Last month the group filled 6 bags of litter; this month only 2. How many fewer bags is that?
exercises.hint: Take the smaller number from the bigger one.
exercises.explain: 6 − 2 = 4 fewer bags: the park is staying cleaner.

exercises.prompt: In many schools in Japan, what do children do each day?
exercises.explain: Many children in Japan clean their own classrooms each day, sharing the work.

exercises.prompt: The United Nations' 17 Global Goals include no hunger and clean water.
exercises.explain: True: the 17 Global Goals, agreed in 2015, include no hunger, clean water and caring for the planet.

exercises.prompt: 4 friends each plant 6 trees, and a grown-up plants 5 more. How many trees are planted?
exercises.hint: Work out the friends' trees first, then add the grown-up's.
